decision.explanation: The subinterval width is Δx=(4−2)/n=2/n. The right endpoints are x_m=2+2m/n, so (x_m+1)^2=(3+2m/n)^2. Multiplying by Δx and summing gives option a.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: What is ${\int }_{2}^{4}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
after.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}f({x}_{m})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{m}=a+mΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{2}^{4}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=(x+1)^{2},$ the lower bound is $a=2$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{4-2}{n}=\frac{2}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{4}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}f({x}_{m})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[f(2+m\cdot \frac{2}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[f(2+\frac{2m}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[{((2+\frac{2m}{n})+1)}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[{(3+\frac{2m}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

a
 limn→∞∑m=1n[(3+2mn)2⋅2n]
b
limn→∞∑m=1n[(3+mn)2⋅1n]
c

limn→∞∑m=1n[(2+2mn)2⋅2n]
e
limn→∞∑m=1n[(2+mn)2⋅1n]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑m=1nf(xm)⋅Δx,

where xm=a+mΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral

∫24(x+1)2dx,

the function is f(x)=(x+1)2, the lower bound is a=2 and the upper bound is b=4. So, we have

Δx=4−2n=2n.

Therefore, ∫24(x+1)2dx=limn→∞∑m=1nf(xm)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑m=1n[f(2+m⋅2n)⋅2n]=limn→∞∑m=1n[f(2+2mn)⋅2n]=limn→∞∑m=1n[((2+2mn)+1)2⋅2n]=limn→∞∑m=1n[(3+2mn)2⋅2n].

content.problem: What is ${\int }_{2}^{4}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
content.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}f({x}_{m})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{m}=a+mΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{2}^{4}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=(x+1)^{2},$ the lower bound is $a=2$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{4-2}{n}=\frac{2}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{4}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}f({x}_{m})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[f(2+m\cdot \frac{2}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[f(2+\frac{2m}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[{((2+\frac{2m}{n})+1)}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[{(3+\frac{2m}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The interval width is Δx=(3−0)/n=3/n. Left endpoints are x_i=3i/n for i=0,...,n−1, giving the sum of e^(3i/n) multiplied by 3/n. Thus option a is correct.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
after.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={e}^{x},$ the lower bound is $a=0,$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(0+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\,\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{3i/n}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
content.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={e}^{x},$ the lower bound is $a=0,$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(0+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\,\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{3i/n}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The width is Δx=(5−1)/n=4/n. Left endpoints are x_i=1+4i/n, so e^(x_i−1)=e^(4i/n). Summing for i=0,...,n−1 gives option e.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: What is ${\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
after.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={e}^{x-1},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-1}{n}=\frac{4}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{4}{n})\,\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{4i}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{1+4i/n-1}\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{4i/n}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1f(xi)⋅Δx,

where Δx=b−an and xi=a+iΔx.

In the definite integral ∫15ex−1dx, the function is f(x)=ex−1, the lower bound is a=1, and the upper bound is b=5. So, we have Δx=5−1n=4n,

and therefore ∫15ex−1dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1f(xi)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[f(1+i⋅4n)⋅4n]=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[f(1+4in)⋅4n]=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[e1+4i/n−1⋅4n]=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[e4i/n⋅4n].

content.problem: What is ${\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
content.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={e}^{x-1},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-1}{n}=\frac{4}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{4}{n})\,\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{4i}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{1+4i/n-1}\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{4i/n}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The subinterval width is Δx=(3−0)/n=3/n. Right endpoints are x_k=3k/n for k=1,...,n, so the sum uses arctan(3k/n) multiplied by 3/n. This is option d.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
after.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(0+k\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
content.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(0+k\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$
